title: Boeing 787 Dreamliner
intro: The Boeing 787 Dreamliner is a modern long-distance passenger jet with two engines. Its cockpit has five large screens, head-up displays for both pilots and a control stand with the thrust levers. Boeing kept the control column and wheel in front of each pilot, although computers fly the aircraft.

areas.name: Glareshield: MCP and HUDs
areas.text: The strip under the windscreen. It holds the autopilot panel and the head-up displays, the glass screens that show flight numbers in front of the pilots' eyes.

panels.name: Glareshield: MCP and HUDs
panels.text: This area holds the mode control panel, where the pilots tell the autopilot what to fly, and the head-up display, a clear glass screen that shows flight numbers in front of the pilot's eyes.
panels.context: The pilots set the targets here after take-off and again for the approach. The autopilot panel works like the one on the Boeing 777.

controls.name: Head-up display (each pilot)
controls.text: This is a clear glass screen in front of the pilot's eyes. It shows speed, height and the path to fly as green marks the pilot sees while looking out of the window.
controls.context: A head-up display (HUD) helps most on landing, since the pilot can look outside and still read the numbers.

controls.name: MCP speed, heading, altitude and V/S
controls.text: These knobs and windows set the speed, the direction, the height and the climb or descent rate that the autopilot should fly.
controls.context: MCP means mode control panel. The pilots dial in what air traffic control asks for and the autopilot follows.

controls.name: A/P, A/T and F/D controls
controls.text: These buttons and switches turn on the autopilot (A/P), the autothrottle (A/T) and the flight director (F/D). The autopilot flies the aircraft, the autothrottle moves the engine power and the flight director shows guide bars on the screen.
controls.context: The pilots switch them on after take-off and keep watching what they do. They can switch them off at any time.

controls.name: EFIS control panels
controls.text: These panels, one for each pilot, set what the pilot's screens show: the air pressure setting, the map type and range, and extra displays.
controls.context: The pilot sets the air pressure here so the altimeter is right, and zooms the map in and out.

areas.name: Five large displays
areas.text: The big screens in the middle of the dashboard: two for each pilot and one in the lower centre.

panels.name: Five large displays
panels.text: Five large screens show everything the pilots need: the flight instruments, the map and the engine and system pages. They replace most of the old round dials.
panels.context: The pilots look at the outer screens when flying and at the inner screens for the route. The lower centre screen is shared.

controls.name: Outboard display (each pilot): PFD
controls.text: This screen in front of each pilot shows the horizon, speed, height and climb rate, with the autopilot modes at the top.
controls.context: PFD means primary flight display. It is the main screen for flying.

controls.name: Inboard display (each pilot): ND / MFD
controls.text: This screen shows the map of the route, and can also show system pages and checklists. Each pilot has one.
controls.context: ND is the navigation display. The pilot can use it for the map or switch it to other pages.

controls.name: Lower centre display
controls.text: This screen shows the engine data and warnings in its upper part, and other pages that either pilot can call up.
controls.context: EICAS is the engine and crew alerting system. It tells the crew about the state of the engines and problems.

controls.name: Landing gear lever

positions.name: UP
positions.text: The wheels fold into the aircraft.

positions.name: DN
positions.text: The wheels are down and locked.

controls.text: This lever folds the wheels away or lowers them. It is in the middle part of the dashboard.
controls.context: The pilot raises the wheels after take-off and lowers them on the approach.

controls.name: Autobrake selector
controls.text: This selector sets how hard the brakes work by themselves after landing, or arms them in case a take-off is stopped.
controls.context: The pilot picks a level before landing, depending on the runway length.

areas.name: Overhead panel
areas.text: The ceiling panel above the pilots, with fewer switches than older airliners because most systems run themselves.

panels.name: Overhead panel
panels.text: This simplified panel holds the switches for the electricity, hydraulic pumps, fire fighting, fuel and lights. Most of the time the computers run these systems by themselves.
panels.context: The pilots set it up in the first minutes in the cockpit and only use it again if a problem comes up.

controls.name: Electrical panel
controls.text: These buttons control the aircraft's electricity: the batteries, the generators and the outside power plug. The 787 runs on electricity instead of using hot air from the engines for many jobs.
controls.context: The pilots use it first when getting into the cockpit. Lights on it show when a source fails.

controls.name: Hydraulic panel
controls.text: These buttons switch the hydraulic pumps on or off. Hydraulics are oil under pressure that moves heavy parts like flaps and wheels.
controls.context: The pilots check them during start-up. A light shows if a pump has a problem.

controls.name: Fire panel
controls.text: This panel handles fires in an engine or the APU, the small helper engine. Pulling a fire handle shuts off its fuel, and it can then fire an extinguisher.
controls.context: It is only used for a real fire, after the fire warning and checklist.

controls.name: Fuel panel
controls.text: These buttons switch the fuel pumps and the cross feed, which lets fuel flow from one side to the other.
controls.context: The pilots switch the pumps on before engine start. The cross feed is used if one side is lower.

controls.name: Exterior lights
controls.text: These switches turn on the lights outside the aircraft: beacon, position lights, strobe flashes, landing and taxi lights.
controls.context: The pilots switch them on in steps, from the red beacon at engine start to the bright landing lights at take-off.

areas.name: Control stand
areas.text: The block between the pilots, with the thrust levers, flap and speed brake levers, fuel switches, the cursor controls and the parking brake.

panels.name: Control stand
panels.text: The control stand sets the engines' power and the shape of the wings. It also has the trackball-type cursor controls with which the pilots point at things on the screens.
panels.context: It is used in every phase of the flight. The thrust levers move by themselves when the autothrottle is on.

controls.name: Thrust levers with reversers
controls.text: These two levers set the engine power. The switches on them start the take-off or go-around power and disconnect the autothrottle. The small piggy-back levers reverse the thrust.
controls.context: Unlike many other fly-by-wire airliners, the Boeing levers move forward and back with the autothrottle, so the pilots can see what the engines do.

controls.name: Speed brake lever
controls.text: This lever opens the speed brakes, panels on the wings that slow the aircraft. They can also be armed to open by themselves on landing.
controls.context: The pilot arms it before landing and may use it in the descent to slow down.

controls.name: Flap lever
controls.text: This lever sets the flaps, the parts of the wing that slide out to give more lift when flying slowly. Each position is a step.
controls.context: The pilot uses a small setting for take-off and larger settings for landing.

controls.name: Fuel control switches

positions.name: RUN
positions.text: Fuel flows and the engine runs.

positions.name: CUTOFF
positions.text: The fuel is cut off and the engine stops.

controls.text: These two switches turn the fuel to each engine on or off, with the positions RUN and CUTOFF.
controls.context: After the engine has started, the pilot moves the switch to RUN. At the end of the flight the switch goes to CUTOFF to stop the engine.

controls.name: Cursor control devices and keypads
controls.text: These are keypads with a trackball or touch area. The pilots use them to point at items on the screens and to type, like a computer mouse and keyboard.
controls.context: They are used to enter the route and to work the pages on the screens.

controls.name: Parking brake lever
controls.text: This lever holds the brakes on when the aircraft stands still.
controls.context: The pilot sets it when parked and releases it before taxiing.

areas.name: Electronic flight bags
areas.text: Screens on the sides of the cockpit that replace the pilots' paper charts and manuals.

panels.name: Electronic flight bags
panels.text: These screens at the sides hold the digital version of the paper maps, charts and manuals the pilots used to carry.
panels.context: The pilots look up airport charts and compute the performance for take-off and landing with them.

controls.name: Captain EFB
controls.text: This screen on the captain's side shows charts and manuals, and helps compute the performance numbers.
controls.context: EFB means electronic flight bag. It replaces the heavy paper bag of old.

controls.name: First officer EFB
controls.text: This is the same kind of screen on the first officer's side, with its own charts and performance pages.
controls.context: Each pilot has one, so both can look up different pages at the same time.

areas.name: Control wheel, thrust levers and pedals
areas.text: The controls for the pilot's hands and feet: the column and wheel, the thrust levers on the control stand and the pedals.

panels.name: Control column and wheel
panels.text: Each pilot has a control column with a wheel. The Boeing keeps this classic design in its fly-by-wire aircraft. The wheel's horn holds buttons for trim, autopilot and radio.
panels.context: The pilot flies with the column and wheel and uses the thumb buttons without letting go.

controls.name: Control column and wheel
controls.text: Pushing the column forward lowers the nose and pulling it back raises it. Turning the wheel left or right rolls the aircraft.
controls.context: The column feels like a mechanical one, with an artificial feel. The computers read its movement and move the control surfaces.

controls.name: Pitch trim switches
controls.text: These two thumb switches work together. Pushing them one way trims the nose down and the other way trims it up.
controls.context: Trim holds the aircraft at a steady tilt without holding the column. The trim also resets the speed the aircraft stays at.

controls.name: Autopilot disengage switch
controls.text: Pressing this thumb button switches the autopilot off. A second press silences the warning sound.
controls.context: The pilot presses it to take over the flying.

controls.name: Microphone switch

positions.name: up
positions.text: Sends on the selected radio while held.

positions.name: down
positions.text: Talks on the flight interphone while held.

positions.name: centre
positions.text: In the middle, nothing is sent.

controls.text: Pushing this switch on the wheel horn one way sends on the radio, the other way talks on the intercom between the crew.
controls.context: The pilot holds it while speaking to the controller.

panels.name: Thrust levers and control stand handles
panels.text: These are the levers on the control stand that the pilot's hand reaches: thrust levers with switches, speed brake, flaps and fuel switches.
panels.context: They are used throughout the flight, from take-off power to reverse thrust and engine shutdown.

controls.name: Thrust lever 1
controls.text: This is the left thrust lever. Pushing it forward gives the left engine more power, pulling it back gives less.
controls.context: The pilot sets the power with it, or leaves it to the autothrottle.

controls.name: Thrust lever 2
controls.text: This is the right thrust lever. It works like the left one for the right engine.
controls.context: The pilot moves both levers together in most cases.

controls.name: TO/GA switches
controls.text: Pressing these switches below the lever knobs starts take-off power or go-around power. The guide bars on the screen change to match.
controls.context: TOGA means take-off and go-around. The pilot presses it at the start of the take-off run or to abandon a landing.

controls.name: Autothrottle disconnect switches
controls.text: Pressing these switches on the outer side of the thrust levers switches the autothrottle off. A second press silences the warning light.
controls.context: The pilot uses it to take over the engine power by hand.

controls.name: Reverse thrust levers
controls.text: These levers on the thrust levers are lifted and pulled back after landing. They turn the engine push forward to help slow the aircraft.
controls.context: The pilot uses reverse thrust right after touchdown, with the brakes.

controls.name: Speed brake lever
controls.text: Moving this lever back opens the speed brakes, moving it forward closes them, and pulling it up arms them for landing.
controls.context: In the air they slow the aircraft. After landing, the full back position opens all the spoilers to press the wheels down.

controls.name: Flap lever
controls.text: Moving this lever forward or back changes the flap setting by one step, between UP, 1, 5, 15, 20, 25 and 30.
controls.context: The pilot sets a small step for take-off and large steps on the approach.

controls.name: Fuel control switch L

positions.name: up
positions.text: RUN: the left engine gets fuel.

positions.name: down
positions.text: CUTOFF: the left engine's fuel is off.

controls.text: This switch below the left thrust lever turns the left engine's fuel on or off. It has a lever lock.
controls.context: The pilot moves it to RUN after the start and to CUTOFF at the end of the flight.

controls.name: Fuel control switch R

positions.name: up
positions.text: RUN: the right engine gets fuel.

positions.name: down
positions.text: CUTOFF: the right engine's fuel is off.

controls.text: This switch below the right thrust lever turns the right engine's fuel on or off. It has a lever lock.
controls.context: It is used the same way as the left one, for the right engine.

controls.name: Parking brake lever
controls.text: Pulling this lever on the left of the control stand sets the parking brake, with the toe brakes pressed. Pressing the toe brakes again releases it.
controls.context: The pilot sets it when parked.

controls.name: Alternate pitch trim levers

positions.name: centre
positions.text: In the middle the alternate trim is off.

controls.text: These levers at the back of the stand trim the nose by hand if the normal trim does not work. Forward trims the nose down and back trims it up.
controls.context: They are the backup way to trim.

panels.name: Landing gear, tiller and pedals
panels.text: The gear lever on the dashboard, the steering wheel at the side and the pedals, used for the ground and the landing.
panels.context: The pilot steers on the ground with the tiller and pedals, and puts the gear down before landing.

controls.name: Landing gear lever
controls.text: Moving this lever up folds the wheels away and moving it down lowers them. It is on the first officer's side of the centre panel.
controls.context: The pilot lowers it on the approach and raises it after take-off.

controls.name: Nosewheel steering tiller
controls.text: Turning this small wheel on the captain's left side steers the front wheel, like a car's steering wheel but with a small wheel.
controls.context: The pilot uses it when taxiing slowly.

controls.name: Rudder pedals
controls.text: Pushing a pedal turns the rudder on the tail. The tops of the pedals are the toe brakes for each side. The pedals also steer the front wheel a few degrees.
controls.context: The pilot keeps the aircraft straight on the runway with them.
